editorials.title: Serious escalation: On the U.S., Russia Sanctions Act and India
editorials.passage:
The U.S. Russia Sanctions Act , now signed into law by President Donald Trump , and its resultant impending tariffs, present a new and substantially different escalation of tensions between the U.S. and India. The law provides the U.S. President the authority to levy tariffs of up to 100% on countries such as India that import large quantities of Russian oil and gas. This is more serious than the penal tariffs that Mr. Trump had levied earlier. The escalation last year of reciprocal tariffs to 50% on India’s import of Russian oil was based on an Executive Order, and could be rescinded through the same method. This latest Act has been passed by the U.S. Congress and so carries a higher order of legal permanence and authority. Mr. Trump will have to justify in writing to Congress any waiver he wants to provide. The 50% tariffs hit Indian exports to the U.S. hard, but the impact was somewhat mitigated by exporters sharing the cost with their American customers. That was, however, a financially devastating and unsustainable bid to retain customers. Sharing a 100% tariff will be impossible for India’s largely micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) exporters. The 100% tariffs are also over and above the 10% ‘forced labour’ tariffs and the 50% Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminium. Indian exports to the U.S. will simply become too uncompetitive should these new tariffs come to pass. India has three options before it: cut Russian oil imports, retain those imports and bear the tariffs, or convince the U.S. to implement a low tariff using the “up to 100%” phrasing of the law.

Continuing with Russian oil imports and bearing the tariffs would be a significant blow to India’s export ambitions and MSMEs. The U.S. is India’s largest export destination, accounting for about 20% of its total goods exports. In any case, historical data have shown that India has usually complied with U.S. pressure to cut oil imports from particular countries, including from Russia, vocal claims of strategic autonomy aside. Finding other sources will be difficult. Russia accounted for more than 51% of India’s oil imports as of July 2026 , while supplies through the Strait of Hormuz remain constrained. India will have to chivvy countries such as Oman to hasten their expansion of alternative ports. The price of oil remains well above $100 a barrel, meaning finding favourable deals with new suppliers will be increasingly difficult. Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal will have much to do during his planned trip to the U.S. at the end of this month for the G-20 Trade Ministerial. There are still 30 days before the U.S. can levy its tariffs. India’s ability to secure a low rate will be a true test of Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s friendship with Mr. Trump.

editorials.title: Antidote to drugs: On the counterfeit medicine racket in Bengaluru, Karnataka
editorials.passage:
With the recent bust of a counterfeit medicine racket in Bengaluru , a public policy issue with broad ramifications for health care in the State has emerged. Centered around Bengaluru, relabelled or fake drugs , including cancer drugs, injections used in the ICU, were supplied to more than 90 hospitals and clinics across the State. The lid was blown off this elaborate scam after incidental raids, near Bidadi in Karnataka on August 18, found suspected fake drugs and expired drugs at a farmhouse which was an unlicensed unit. The consignment had a label value of ₹5 crore. Investigators said that the farmhouse was used in an illicit drug operation — involving the repacking of fake and expired drugs as fresh consignments, with altered expiry dates, and as expensive, imported branded drugs — which were then sold at massive discounts. The State later formed a Special Investigation Team to trace the wider network. While exploring the distribution mechanism, investigators found that the network had been supplying these drugs to over 90 hospitals in the State, in cahoots with a pharmacy in Bengaluru, indicating that a network was thriving well before the bust. A few persons have been arrested and the police are on the tail of another who is not in the country at present. The impunity with which the scamsters were operating is an indication of the unreliable scrutiny of the quality of drugs in the market. The biggest concern, however, is patient safety, given that these are drugs that can save lives and are marked out for time-sensitive usage. Also being examined are possible inter-State links, as investigators have launched a complete review of the supply chain. The illicit channels through which private hospitals bought and used these drugs, including possible complicity in the private hospital network, are under scrutiny.

With alarming regularity, issues to do with poor quality, spurious, fake or expired drugs hit the headlines in India. For a nation that zealously aspires to become the ‘pharmacy of the world’, India struggles to match its ambition with adequate and stringent monitoring and quality control systems. The question of drug quality is particularly significant as fake or spurious drugs can cause immediate adverse reactions, lead to severe disabilities, and even death. Recent incidents of contaminated cough syrups causing deaths, not only in India, but across the world, have further highlighted these woefully inadequate systems and consistently dented the pride of the “Make in India” campaign. Irrespective of whether India becomes the pharmacy of the world, there is a pressing need to make sure that drugs and medical supplies made in the country fulfil the highest quality standards.

editorials.title: Let US polls season play out to parry Trump's tariff threat
editorials.passage: With US President Donald Trump signing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act shortly after Congress cleared it, policy watchers suspect he would use it to nudge India towards a bilateral trade agreement that is yet to be concluded. Just the other day, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said India was waiting for Washington to offer a preferential rate in comparison to the competition. But that flexibility and sovereignty in decision-making could be under test, as the sanctions Act authorises Trump to impose up to 100 percent tariff on India and four other big buyers of Russian energy, arguing their decisions are fueling President Vladimir Putin’s war machine against Ukraine. Why, then, target India alone?Data put out by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air shows that between December 2022 and August 2026, China imported about 50 percent of Russia’s crude, India 37 percent, while Turkey and the European Union were next in the pecking order at 5 percent each. With Trump expected to treat Xi Jinping with pomp at the White House this week, chances of playing the tariff game with the Chinese President are next to negligible. He notably did not penalise Beijing when he doubled the levy on New Delhi to 50 percent last year over Russian buy before he rolled it back. Another round of tariffs on India could draw a similar cold stare. As for Turkey and the EU, their volumes of Russian imports are way too small compared to India’s exposure..India’s initial terse response to the legislation, warning that the measures could have implications for both bilateral ties and global energy markets, suggested it was prepared for any eventuality. Energy security for 1.4 billion citizens is paramount, the foreign office said, adding it would continue to pursue this objective through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics. Interestingly, India had largely tapered off Russian crude imports earlier this year before Trump’s disastrous war with Iran opened that spigot once again. editorials.title: Trust renewal needed in life-saving healthcare
editorials.passage: The supply of spurious life-saving medicines to hospitals, clinics and medical shops in Bengaluru and surrounding areas threatens not only the state’s healthcare system, but lives across India too. Probes have revealed that a bulk of these fake drugs was supplied from locations in Himachal Pradesh and Telangana. Five persons have so far been arrested in the case, while the kingpin is said to be holed up in Azerbaijan.The police, along with officials from Karnataka’s Food and Drug Administration, raided a farmhouse near Bidadi on Bengaluru’s outskirts on August 18 and seized ₹4.91 crore worth of outdated drugs. Preliminary inquiries revealed that these medicines past their use-by dates were repackaged using names of globally reputed pharma manufacturers. But the precise extent of this racket across Karnataka and India is yet to be assessed. The state government has since constituted a special investigations team for the case.  The alarming nature of this scam lies in the fact that the largest component of the spurious drugs seized was Cefiavigent 2.5 injection, pushed as a cancer-related critical-care medication. There were as many as 5,640 vials seized, valued at ₹3.38 crore of the total ₹4.91-crore bust. As the seized vials are linked to counterfeit and unverified manufacturing operations with forged labels and expired components, health authorities have blocked their batch numbers on official portals..Considering that the racket involves a sprawling nationwide network with the possibility of extending to several other states, Karnataka Health Minister U T Khader has written to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation under the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare seeking federal surveillance officials to be deputed to help Karnataka’s ongoing SIT probe to identify the precise nature and spread of the racket.The alarm is not limited to casting aspersions on India’s ₹4.72-lakh-crore pharma industry, ranked third globally, and threatening exports worth ₹2.74 lakh crore; it extends to the potentially worrisome impact on further corrosion of public faith in the country’s healthcare system.The onus of busting this—and similar other rackets—must squarely lie with both the Centre and the states to punish the guilty and build credible deterrence against such nefarious activities. editorials.title: Quick Take | Drinking karma-cola
editorials.passage: Two recent events at two corners of the country linked back to previous regimes in diametrically opposite ways. There was a heartwarming moment in Kerala when Congress MLA Sebastian M J invited his predecessor from the Poonjar Assembly constituency, Sebastian Kulathunkal of the Congress(M), a member of the rival LDF coalition, to inaugurate a bridge that had been sanctioned with the latter’s MLA funds. In this rare public show of courtesy in politics, the incumbent’s name was kept off the commemorative plaque. Meanwhile, a 2,000-page chargesheet filed on a deadly warehouse collapse in Kolkata’s Taratola named, among the seven accused, a mayor’s aide from the previous regime. editorials.title: Many faces of malnutrition
editorials.passage:
Nutrition as a measure of welfare is significantly correlated with income. It is indeed a “primary good” of welfare. The term “malnutrition” is often loosely used by laymen without paying adequate attention to its meaning. Even among biologists and nutritionists there is no consensus on the basic question of how malnutrition should be defined and by which yardstick it should be measured. In nutrition literature, there is also no universally accepted terminology to differentiate various types of nutritional deficiencies. 

However, the term malnutrition is used in relation to undernutrition (protein- energy malnutrition-PEM), overnutrition (consumption of excessive calories) and also hidden hunger (micronutrient deficiency). Malnutrition is the bigger as well as the harder problem to deal with. It is not easy to think of any social problem in the contemporary world that deserves greater attention than the foggy adversity of chronic and widespread malnutrition. According to Nobel laureate Amartya Sen while famine kills millions of people with dramatic suddenness, chronic malnutrition causes termination of many more lives. 

Persistent malnutrition also blights the existence of people who may not die as a result of it but whose ability to lead and secure, productive and happy lives is severely afflicted by debilitation and morbidity. All this happens without the climatic swiftness of famine, and generally does not stimulate visual empathy and sympathetic outbursts that famines can generate with the help of public media. Even the exact magnitude and intensity of malnutrition in different countries of the world remain obscured from public view. The fact is that more people die from malnutrition than from famines, and also that many more people lead severely constrained lives as a result of it. 

There is no perfect way, and never will be, of defining and measuring malnutrition. Predominantly, there are only two data sets that can be consulted. One is from the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) and the other from the World Health Organization (WHO). The FAO approach is designed merely for estimating the proportion of the population that is malnourished; it cannot be used for identifying malnourished households or individuals. However, the magnitude of malnutrition at the individual level can be assessed through anthropometric measures as devised by WHO. 

WHO’s method for ascertaining the status of malnutrition is considered to have many advantages over other approaches since body measurements are sensitive to even minor levels of malnutrition, biochemical and clinical indicators. Anthropometric measures are stunting (low height-for-age), wasting (low weight-for-height) and underweight (low weight-for-age). While wasting is usually reversible with appropriate nutrition and medical care, underweight itself is also reversible. However, stunting in childhood indicates chronic malnutrition and has an irreversible effect on health and human development. Surprisingly, a recent study points to a troubling consequence: climate change may be contributing to a “clinically stunted” future. Growth stunting in childhood is a risk factor for increased mortality, poor cognitive and motor development, and other impairments in function. 

Children who have been severely malnourished in early years suffer a later reduction in IQ by as many as 15 points, significantly affecting schooling achievement and increasing the risks of drop-out or repeat grades. Moreover, stunting usually persists, leading to smaller size and poorer performance in adulthood. Stunting along with low birth weight (LBW), is also a risk factor for adult chronic diseases. However, poverty and stunting set a vicious cycle [poverty è low intake of food & nutrientsèmalnutritionèstunted development of childrenèsmall body size of adultsèimpaired productivityèlow earning capacityèpoverty]. Height is a definite indicator of good health or healthy growth. 

Height deficit reflects a substantial measure of foregone well-being vis-à-vis human capital at a microeconomic level. According to the World Bank, one per cent loss in adult height due to childhood stunting is associated with a 1.4 per cent loss in economic productivity. Stunted children can earn up to 20 per cent less as adults. Stunting is already a major public health challenge in India. The World Bank Group’s latest report entitled “Building Human capital ~ Where it Matters” has assessed the state of human capital in the world. Human capital has been defined as “people’s health, skills and knowledge”. One major salient finding of the assessment is that “Human Capital” accumulation has stagnated in many low and middle-income countries. 

India belongs to this group. Adult height across these countries is not increasing; rather it has remained stagnant or has declined over decades. The report also mentioned that, “an adult of sub-Saharan Africa born in 1996 is 3 centimeters shorter than the average adult born in 1966.” The average adult height for Indians born in 1966 and 1996 remains the same, or is slightly on the decline. Now, it appears that percentage of stunted children is shrinking in India as revealed from data recorded in consecutive National Family Health Surveys: NFHS-3 (2005-06) ~ 48 per cent; NFHS-4 (2015-16) ~ 38.4 per cent; NFHS-5 (2019-21) ~ 35.5 per cent; NFHS-6 (2025-26) ~ 29.3 per cent. 

Human capital has also grown at 1.1 per cent in the last decade in India, while the figure is 4 per cent for high-income countries and 3 per cent for upper- middle-countries like China, Chile and Brazil. Our target should be at least 2.5 per cent. However, to prevent stunting and loss of human capital, steps should be taken to strengthen maternal nutrition, healthcare access, and early childhood stimulation. The consequence of nutritional deprivation tends to pass on across generations in the form of a vicious cycle, given that there is no external intervention from institutions of society. 

For example, the risk of malnutrition is found to be higher among children whose mothers suffer from chronic energy deficiency disorders, which is again dependent on the mother’s childhood nutritional status, thus creating a mother-child-mother malnutrition cycle among the poorer sections of society. Impoverishment due to nutritional deprivation is defined as the umbrella term of malnutrition. The impact of malnutrition on future life chances starts before birth. 

In 1995, the British Medical Journal referred to Dr. David J. P. Barker’s Hypothesis ~ also known as Fetal Origins of Adult Diseases (FOAD)- which posits that maternal dietary imbalances at critical periods of development of the womb can trigger an adaptive redistribution of fetal resources (including growth retardation). Such adaptations affect fetal structure and metabolism in ways that predispose the individual to later cardiovascular and endocrine diseases. Dr. Barkar, an influential English physician and epidemiologist, working with historical data from England, noticed that regions with higher infant mortality rates in the 1920s had more deaths from heart disease in the 1970s. He connected the dots: poor foetal nutrition programmes the body for thrift. A foetus that “learns” it is growing in a starved environment slows down metabolism, alters organs development, and conserves fat. 

But when it is later exposed to calorie-rich food, these programmed adaptations backfire ~ leading to conditions like type 2 diabetes and hypertension. What Barker proposed was that diabetes, hypertension, and heart diseases do not begin in adulthood but in the wombs of malnourished mothers. And not merely from genes but also a fetus's biological response to the mother’s diet. The most common causes of poor growth in developing countries at the immediate level include poor maternal nutritional status at conception and in- utero malnutrition, inadequate breastfeeding, delayed complementary feeding for infants and/or inadequate quality or quantity of complementary feeding, impaired absorption of nutrients due to intestinal infections or parasites; or usually a combination of these problems. 

The first 1000 days of human life ~ from conception to a child’s second birthday ~ represent a golden window of opportunity for future growth and development. During this period, the brain grows at a pace that is never repeated in life, laying the groundwork for learning, behavior, and lifelong health. Just like scaffolding lends support for each floor of a building during construction, each stage of brain development similarly helps build the next one. In these formative 1,000 days, the brain forms millions of neural connections at a rapid pace, reaching 80 per cent of its adult size by age two. 

This is when the foundations of cognitive skill, language, emotional regulation, and social development are laid. At the same time, organs, bones, and muscles are developing rapidly. Adequate nutrition and stimulation are essential to ensure the process continues smoothly, helping to build a stronger immune system and reduce risk of diseases later in life. Nutritional deprivation is a critical issue often intertwined with poverty and economic distress. Limited food choices for the poor typically cripple their nutritional status, resulting in disparities in lower and middle-income countries. 

In India, findings indicate that districts in states such as Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, and Maharashtra still face extreme levels of nutritional deprivation, with over 40 per cent of districts in these states experiencing “extreme deprivation” in 2019-21. Conversely, states like MP (rural) and West Bengal (urban) have made notable progress, lifting a substantial 40 per cent and 30 per cent of their districts out of “extreme deprivation”. Improving education among women, encouraging diversified diets and providing easier access to healthcare are some of the ways in which India can achieve nutritional security by 2030. Food and nutrition are human rights, enshrined in various conventions. Governments have a duty to ensure that these dimensions of human well-being are realized. 

  
(The writer is a retired IAS officer)

editorials.title: From water stress to water resilience
editorials.passage:
Water under pins civilisation, prosperity, food security, social equity and ecological well-being. Yet it is under growing strain. Climate change is disrupting rainfall patterns, intensifying floods and droughts, accelerating glacial melt and increasing the frequency of extreme hydrological events. Recent floods, cloudbursts and landslides in neighbouring Nepal show that water-related risks are no longer distant. 

As New Delhi prepares to host the 9th India International Water Week (IIWW-2026) from 22 to 26 September under the theme “Climate Resilient Water Management,” the question is not whether water systems need to adapt to climate change. It is how rapidly and comprehensively they can do so. For India, water security is inseparable from the journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047. Inclusive prosperity cannot endure if water resources remain fragile, polluted or inefficiently managed. 

The task is integrated stewardship - from catchment to consumer and source to safe reuse. India’s water challenges are interconnected. Erratic rainfall brings both scarcity and destructive excess, sometimes in the same region. Groundwater depletion threatens farms and drinking-water supplies; rapid urbanisation adds demand while reducing recharge areas; and pollution reduces the volume of water that is safely usable. Ageing infrastructure, competing demands and uneven capacity add to the pressure. No single intervention can address this challenge. Water needs to be managed as a connected system of catchments, rivers, aquifers, reservoirs, farms, cities, industries and communities. 

That calls for aligning conservation, augmentation, efficiency, infrastructure, data, regulation and public participation. India has already begun this transition. Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari: Catch the Rain places communities at the centre of water conservation, rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge and water-body rejuvenation. Its message - “Catch the Rain, Where It Falls, When It Falls” - recognises that durable water security is strengthened when citizens, local bodies, farmers and panchayats act alongside government. Agriculture remains central to this effort. 

As the largest user of water, it can become more efficient and climate resilient through micro-irrigation, improved on-farm water management and the wider objectives of “Har Khet Ko Pani” and “Per Drop More Crop” under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana. Groundwater management can likewise draw on scientif ic assessment, aquifer understanding, demand management and community-led planning. India is also strengthening the safety, surveillance and ecological health of its water systems. The Dam Safety Act, 2021, and the Dam Rehabilitation and Improvement Project provide an institutional and engineering framework to improve dam safety and performance, particularly amid ageing infrastructure, erratic inflows and extreme events. 

The National Hydrology Project is reinforcing the digital foundation of water governance through timely and reliable water-resources data and decision-support tools. Better data can support forecasting, reservoir operations, flood management and basin planning. River restoration should accompany infrastructure development. Namami Gange has linked pollution abatement with the conservation and rejuvenation of the Ganga. Future efforts can place sustained focus on wastewater treatment, ecological flows, tributaries, wetlands, non-point pollution and the restoration of natural river functions. 

India also has an opportunity to advance a circular water economy. Treated wastewater can increasingly serve non-potable uses in industry, agriculture, horticulture, construction, landscaping and municipal services, subject to suitable quality standards and safeguards. This can reduce freshwater pressure, improve urban resilience and enable resource recovery. Water management can further evolve from localised, project-specific interventions to integrated basin-scale planning. Coordinated surface- and groundwater management, upstreamdownstream cooperation, modernised infrastructure, demand management and carefully assessed inter-basin interventions can support resilience, equity and ecological integrity. IIWW-2026 arrives at a consequential moment. 

It will bring together policymakers, scientists, practitioners, innovators, industry and international partners through plenaries, country forums, technical sessions, exhibitions and the Second International WASH Conference. Its agenda includes urban flooding, digital technologies, groundwater, river resilience and climate adaptation. The event can be a platform for partnerships, scalable solutions and measurable commitments. Three outcomes deserve attention. First, it can accelerate the responsible use of artificial intelligence for hydrological forecasting, remote sensing for glacial lake outburst flo o d monitoring , advance d water-quality surveillance and digital basin modelling. 

Technology is most useful when it complements capable institutions and local knowledge. Second, it can help scale circular wastewater systems and viable models for water reuse. This will benefit from appropriate standards, reliable operations, clear institutional responsibility and sustainable financing. Demonstrations can become replicable models for cities, industrial clusters, farms and rural settlements. Third, IIWW-2026 can narrow the gap between scientific institutions, businesses, government agencies and village panchayats. 

Blended finance, outcome-based investment, public-private partnerships and community ownership can help innovations move from laboratories and pilot projects into routine practice. There is no single answer to India’s water challenge. Large infrastructure will remain relevant in many contexts, while local harvesting, aquifer recharge, conservation and behavioural change remain equally indispensable. Technology cannot compensate for weak governance, and community participation cannot replace sound engineering. 

Progress lies in combining infrastructure, institutions, science and public action. The climate challenge tests our collective resolve. Yet scientific rigour, policy foresight, accountable institutions and meaningful community participation can turn water from a source of vulnerability into an engine of sustainable prosperity. IIWW-2026 is India’s appeal to the world to join hands in collaboration, innovation and shared action for a water-secure, climate-resilient and equitable future for all. 

(The writer is Secretary, Water Resources, Government of India)

editorials.title: Oil and leverage
editorials.passage:
India’s Russian oil purchases have exposed a contradiction in its economic diplomacy: the pursuit of affordable energy can strengthen national interests while creating vulnerabilities that another power can exploit. The US House of Representatives’ passage of legislation authorising President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries buying Russian oil and gas brings that contradiction into sharp focus. Although the measure requires Trump’s signature, the threat alone raises questions about India’s trade relations, energy security and strategic autonomy. 

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Indian refiners have benefited from crude supplies redirected from Western markets. The purchases helped contain import costs in an economy heavily dependent on overseas energy. But Russia’s growing share of Indian imports has created an exposure extending beyond the oil sector. The United States is a major destination for Indian exports, including pharmaceuticals, electronics, textiles and machinery. Punitive tariffs could therefore affect employment, investment and the balance of payments. The danger is that energy dependence could become bargaining currency in negotiations over wider economic interests. 

If access to the American market is made conditional on India’s energy choices or trade concessions, commercial diplomacy risks becoming an exercise in unequal leverage. India should neither abandon Russian crude to avoid confrontation nor purchase it regardless of cost. The calculation must include discounts, freight, insurance, refinery compatibility and potential damage to exports. A saving at the refinery gate may prove costly when wider economic consequences are considered. The distinction between defending freedom of choice and becoming dependent on a particular supplier is crucial. 

Replacing Russian oil with supplies from elsewhere will not automatically eliminate vulnerability, particularly when alternative routes pass through conflict-prone regions. India’s limited strategic petroleum reserves underline the need for a more durable energy policy. Diversification requires investment in storage, infrastructure capable of processing different crude grades and a wider network of reliable suppliers. Dependence on imported liquefied petroleum gas also makes energy security a matter of household economic stability. China’s position offers a significant contrast. 

Its centrality to global supply chains and the scale of its economic relationship with the US may give Beijing greater capacity to absorb or counter American pressure. India cannot assume that its expanding trade partnerships provide equal protection. The proposed legislation also raises a broader question about the international economic order. When access to a powerful country’s market becomes an instrument for influencing another state’s foreign policy, the boundary between trade and geopolitical coercion becomes blurred. 

Delhi should negotiate firmly with Washington while retaining the flexibility to buy Russian crude when commercially justified. It must also avoid allowing short-term savings to obscure the need to reduce dependence on individual suppliers and export markets. Strategic autonomy cannot rest on declarations alone. It requires diversified energy supplies, adequate reserves and an economy resilient enough to withstand external pressure. India’s challenge is not simply to decide where to buy oil, but to build the capacity to make that decision without economic coercion.

editorials.title: Inflation’s Trap
editorials.passage:
The world had begun to believe that the inflation crisis was receding. Central banks had reduced interest rates, supply chains had recovered and price pressures had eased. But the latest developments in the United States and Britain suggest that the struggle to restore price stability is far from over. The danger is no longer simply that inflation will remain high, but that efforts to contain it could undermine economic growth. 

The Federal Reserve’s decision to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point, to 3.75-4.5 per cent, marks its first increase in more than three years. The move came despite President Donald Trump’s repeated demands for lower borrowing costs. Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has argued that inflation remains too high, while the central bank’s projections indicate the possibility of further increases. The decision underlines the tension between the political attraction of cheaper credit and the institutional responsibility to contain inflation. 

Britain presents a related but more complicated picture. The Bank of England has held its rate at 3.75 per cent, but three of its nine monetary policymakers favoured an increase. Governor Andrew Bailey has warned that prolonged energy-price volatility could require tighter policy. The Bank also expects inflation to rise more sharply than previously anticipated, even as it has upgraded its near-term growth forecast. These decisions reflect a common predicament. The conflict in West Asia has disrupted energy supplies, pushed up fuel costs and threatens to spread inflation. 

Central banks cannot end wars or increase oil supplies. They can, however, restrain demand in an attempt to prevent higher costs from becoming embedded in wages and prices. That remedy carries its own risks. Higher rates increase mortgage repayments and the cost of business finance, potentially discouraging investment and consumption. Governments face higher borrowing costs, while already struggling households have less room to absorb further increases. The Bank of England’s decision to slow its government-bond sales also illustrates the difficulty of managing inflation alongside financial-market pressures. The implications extend beyond advanced economies. 

Countries dependent on imported energy face additional pressure on currencies, public finances and household purchasing power. India, where retail inflation has recently increased, must weigh these risks as the Reserve Bank of India assesses whether price pressures are temporary or becoming more persistent. Yet the choices facing central banks are not identical. A rate increase may be justified where inflation is broadening, but could be counterproductive if higher prices are confined to a temporary supply shock. 

The crucial distinction is whether rising energy costs are beginning to influence the wider economy. The deeper lesson is that inflation cannot be managed through interest rates alone. Energy security, resilient supply chains and credible fiscal policies matter too. Without them, monetary authorities may repeatedly be forced to suppress demand in response to disruptions they cannot control. The world’s inflation problem is therefore also a growth problem ~ and an institutional one. Central banks must defend price stability without inflicting avoidable economic damage.

editorials.title: A new map
editorials.passage:
Sometimes, geography speaks more eloquently than politics. The catastrophe that descended through the high Himalaya on August 26 is an example.

Early reports called it an earthquake, then a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF). The scientific picture that has since emerged is both more complex and more instructive. A massive section of rock and glacial ice appears to have detached from the north face of Langtang Lirung in Nepal. Its impact generated a seismic signal equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. The ensuing mass of rock, ice, water and debris entered the Lhende Khola river system and travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream, devastating communities in Nepal and overwhelming Gyirong on the Tibetan side of the frontier.

In a quick countdown to disaster, geology became glaciology, glaciology became hydrology, and hydrology translated into catastrophe.

Himalayan disasters are classified separately by habit: earthquakes, landslides, avalanches, cloudbursts, GLOFs. The mountains recognise no such taxonomy. A collapsing slope can dislodge a glacier; an avalanche can enter a river; debris can temporarily obstruct water; intense rainfall can destabilise already fragile terrain. Both the trigger and the events that follow connect together.

Langtang is therefore best understood as a cascading hazard. And for India it should change how we think about the Himalaya.

Having travelled extensively through these mountains and across the Tibetan plateau, what stays with one is their immense verticality: great heights falling abruptly into confined valleys, rivers compressed into narrow gorges, roads and settlements occupying slender ribbons of habitable land. When something gives way at those elevations, gravity becomes an elemental force.

Climate change adds another layer of uncertainty. Glaciers are retreating; glacial lakes are changing; warming affects relationships among ice, permafrost and rock. It is true that we should not reduce every Himalayan disaster to climate change. These are young, unstable and seismically active mountains. But the physical conditions within which natural hazards occur are undoubtedly changing.

India has already received warnings: Kedarnath in 2013, Chamoli in 2021 and South Lhonak in Sikkim in 2023. Their immediate causes differed. The underlying message did not. Infrastructure placed in narrow Himalayan valleys is exposed not merely to local conditions but to events originating many kilometres and thousands of metres above it.

The aftermath in Nepal now illustrates this with devastating clarity. More than a dozen hydropower projects were damaged. Nepal, normally an electricity exporter to India, has had to reverse the flow and import up to 654 MW of Indian power to compensate for lost generation. A horrifying collapse in one mountain catchment has thus travelled, in effect, into the electricity grids and economies of neighbouring states.

The answer is not to stop Himalayan development. Mountain communities need roads, power, communications and livelihoods. India has legitimate strategic reasons for improving border infrastructure. But the unit of risk assessment must change.

The safety of a dam, bridge, tunnel or highway cannot be judged only at the point where it is built. What glaciers lie upstream? Which slopes are unstable? Where might rock or ice block a river? How would floodwater, debris or sediment move through the catchment?

The catchment, rather than the construction site, must increasingly become the unit of Himalayan risk assessment.

Nor can every slope and glacier be watched with the same intensity. The more practical approach, advocated by Nithiyanandam Yogeswaran of the Takshashila Institution, is to identify critical locations where failure would have serious downstream consequences and concentrate scientific observation there. Satellites, radar, InSAR, LiDAR, seismic instruments, river gauges and high-altitude weather stations can collectively reveal much that no single technology can.

Yet technology is not without its limits. Remote sensing may show a slope moving or a glacier changing. It cannot always tell us when collapse will occur. Nor can a satellite disclose dam operating rules, subsurface geological measurements or what instruments on the ground are recording at a particular moment.

India therefore needs a two-track approach to Himalayan knowledge.

First, it should possess the sovereign capability to observe and analyse as much as possible for itself — through satellites, seismic networks, remote sensing and open-source geospatial intelligence. Second, it must seek from neighbouring states precisely the information that cannot be acquired from space.

The first is national capability. The second requires transboundary cooperation. That brings us inevitably to China. China’s vast hydropower project on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo sharpens these questions. The Great Bend is among the most geologically dramatic landscapes on earth: deeply incised, seismically active and vulnerable to landslides. The sensible question is neither whether the project is inherently catastrophic nor whether general assurances of safety should satisfy India. It is whether India knows enough about upstream geology, slope stability, sediment movement, extreme-flow scenarios and project operations to assess downstream risk intelligently.

India can discover much independently. But engineering specifications, environmental assessments, reservoir operations and real-time ground observations require another form of transparency.

And China should have an interest in such cooperation. Beijing has invested enormously in transforming Tibet through roads, railways, airports, dams and logistics hubs, including infrastructure intended to connect the plateau more closely with Nepal and South Asia. The destruction at Gyirong demonstrated that Chinese strategic infrastructure is vulnerable to the same Himalayan geology.

There is, amid competition and mistrust, an unusual community of interest: India and China both have much to lose from understanding these mountains badly.

Nepal’s experience makes the point still more sharply. Nepalese and Chinese officials had met in Kathmandu in May to discuss precisely the need for cooperation on floods, weather and glacier-related hazards. After the disaster, Kathmandu renewed its call for better data and earlier warnings. The problem, therefore, is no longer recognising the need. It is converting dialogue into systems capable of acting at the speed of a disaster.

India, China and Nepal should establish protocols under which exceptional upstream events — dangerous glacial movement, landslides, river blockages, abnormal seismic signals and extreme precipitation — automatically trigger notification across borders. Where observations have clear downstream relevance, scientific data should not have to travel through the full machinery of diplomacy before reaching people in danger.

This cooperation need not await the restoration of strategic trust. The India-China boundary question remains unresolved. Environmental cooperation cannot substitute for a settlement. But the recent political thaw, including the Narendra Modi-Xi Jinping meeting in Delhi, offers an opportunity to create a narrowly insulated sphere of scientific cooperation whose usefulness does not depend on the ambient temperature of the larger relationship.

For decades, India has understood Himalayan security principally in territorial terms: frontiers to defend, passes to watch, roads to build, boundaries to negotiate. That remains indispensable. However, the August catastrophe tells us that another map must sit beside the geopolitical one. On that map, Himalayan security has three interlocking dimensions: ecological security, infrastructure security and knowledge security.

Knowledge security means possessing the ability to see what is changing in the mountains, understand what those changes signify, obtain information that only neighbours can provide, and act before uncertainty becomes catastrophe.

The Himalaya is one physical system divided by political boundaries. India and China may disagree profoundly about where their frontier lies. The glaciers and rivers on either side are indifferent to that disagreement. Disasters do not stop at the Line of Actual Control. A river does not consult a political map.

Human beings draw borders because borders matter. But these mountain ranges are oblivious to this. While tensions along borders and LACs will persist, the greatest threat is hiding in plain sight waiting to come not across the frontier, but down the mountain.

Nirupama Rao is a former foreign secretary. The views expressed are personal

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Only children in China are 18.4% likelier to marry fellow only children
editorials.passage:
Sir — A new study suggests only children in China are 18.4% likelier to marry fellow only children. The preference reveals how family structure shapes intimacy. Having grown up as the sole focus of parental attention and inheritance, many may hesitate to enter households with rival heirs and divided loyalties. This matters as Chinese marriage registrations continue to tumble. Indian suitors, though, are spared such arithmetic. Here, marriage still follows the Sooraj Barjatya script: two people wed along with parents, siblings, cousins, uncles and aunts. The family tree comes bundled with the vows.

Sir — The Bharatiya Janata Party marked the 76th birthday of the prime minister, Narendra Modi, by imposing elaborate programmes on the nation. Gujarat alone lit 76,000 lamps alongside holding cultural events. Such extravagance appears to be an exercise in flattery, reminiscent of the personality cult surrounding North Korea’s leaders. It also consumes money, time and administrative energy better spent elsewhere. Modi could curb this spectacle if he wished. As Norman Vincent Peale observed, “The trouble with most of us is that we would rather be ruined by praise than saved by criticism.” Is the prime minister listening?

Avinash Godboley, Dewas, Madhya Pradesh

Sir — By all accounts, the BJP government in Bengal is struggling to get a grip on governance in the state. Why, then, should taxpayers’ money be spent celebrating Narendra Modi’s birthday? Such expenditure is difficult to justify. The bigger question on everyone’s minds is whether the time come for Modi to make way for a younger prime minister?

Sir — The BJP’s celebration of the prime minister’s birthday amidst severe flooding in Bihar was insensitive. Nearly 50 lakh people across 15 districts have been affected and thousands have been displaced. Yet, administrative machinery was deployed for programmes such as “Ashirwad Ka Diya” and the “Seva Sankalp Abhiyan”. At a time when many flood victims are struggling to cook one square meal a day, mass lamp-lighting is particularly jarring. The BJP government should have directed its resources towards food, medicines and the rehabilitation of affected families.

Sir — Narendra Modi turned 76 on September 17. BJP governments across the country celebrated the occasion with campaigns and welfare programmes. Modi’s energy and commitment to public life challenge stereotypes about ageing and demonstrate that advancing years need not diminish one’s enthusiasm or capacity for work.

Sir — The United States of America’s admission that it has deployed On-Orbit Space-Control Weapons (OOSCW) is a dangerous escalation in the militarisation of space. China has warned against turning space into a battlefield, while Russia has called for its demilitarisation. Yet both countries either already possess or are developing counter-space capabilities. American deployments could therefore provoke rival powers into expanding their own arsenals. Weapons have already caused untold destruction on Earth. Outer space should remain a domain of international cooperation rather than become another theatre of conflict.

Gregory Fernandes, Mumbai

Sir — International law does not prohibit every kind of weapon in space. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit, yet does not expressly outlaw conventional weapons. The US has now confirmed the deployment of OOSCW, ostensibly to protect its satellites. This disclosure could accelerate an expensive arms race. At a time when millions lack food, healthcare and education, devoting vast resources to orbital warfare is indefensible. Has humanity acquired the means to explore space merely to carry its oldest folly there?

Jang Bahadur Singh, Jamshedpur

Sir — The US’s revelation that it has deployed OOSCW raises the spectre of a perilous arms race. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits weapons of mass destruction in orbit and restricts military activity on celestial bodies, but leaves conventional orbital weapons largely unregulated. Invoking unspecified threats from adversaries cannot justify developments that may provoke further militarisation. Outer space is a shared domain and must not become another theatre of geopolitical confrontation. National-security concerns demand international rules and restraint, not an unchecked competition for orbital dominance.

M. Jeyaram, Sholavandan, Tamil Nadu

Sir — Any effort to militarise space by the US will no doubt be followed by similar attempts by China and Russia, not to mention other countries. Is this the beginning of a new arms race? This must be avoided at all costs.

editorials.title: Grim trigger
editorials.passage:
The Constitution was not conceived as a document of convenience. It is a charter of restraint that limits State power in the face of overwhelming public sentiment. Article 21 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law. Over the years, the Supreme Court has interpreted this guarantee to mean a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable.

This constitutional pledge should not be misunderstood as one that diminishes the extraordinary challenges faced by India’s police forces. Police personnel routinely confront terrorists, organised crime syndicates, armed offenders and violent criminals under hazardous circumstances. The law recognises the right of private defence and permits the use of proportionate force whenever necessary to protect life or prevent grave harm.

Genuine encounters arising out of lawful self-defence are thus distinguishable from allegations of extra-judicial executions. However, every encounter resulting in death must be subjected to independent legal scrutiny because the use of lethal State force is an exceptional exercise of executive power.

In People’s Union for Civil Liberties vs State of Maharashtra , the Supreme Court laid down 16 mandatory guidelines governing police encounters. The court directed compulsory registration of an FIR, investigation by an independent agency, magisterial inquiry, forensic examination, preservation of evidence, reporting to the National Human Rights Commission, and judicial oversight wherever necessary.

The issue has acquired renewed relevance. In Arif Md. Yeasin Jwadder vs State of Assam (2025), the Supreme Court dealt with allegations arising out of 171 police encounter incidents reported between May 2021 and August 2022. According to affidavits filed by the Assam government itself, these incidents resulted in 56 deaths, including four custodial deaths, and 145 injuries. The court reaffirmed that allegations involving encounter deaths must be subjected to an independent and impartial inquiry and directed the Assam Human Rights Commission to conduct a time-bound investigation while ensuring legal aid for victims. It also reiterated that the safeguards laid down in PUCL vs State of Maharashtra are mandatory.

The significance of this decision extends beyond Assam. It reiterates a constitutional truth: accountability strengthens policing rather than undermining it.

Official data demonstrate why this debate deserves sustained attention. Analyses based on NHRC records indicate that approximately 813 encounter-related cases were registered across India between 2016-17 and 2021-22. A substantial number of inquiries remained pending, while convictions of officials were negligible.

The growing public endorsement of encounter policing also reflects a deeper institutional crisis. India’s criminal justice system continues to grapple with delayed investigations, mounting judicial arrears, inadequate forensic infrastructure, witness intimidation and prolonged trials. When citizens begin to perceive encounters as a substitute for judicial determination, the problem lies not merely with policing but with the broader administration of justice.

The debate is not between public safety and individual rights. It is between two competing visions of justice. One places faith in constitutional institutions, due process, and judicial determination. The other risks allowing executive power to become the arbiter of guilt.

editorials.title: Brand hurt: Editorial on Tata’s boardroom battle and the cost of corporate discord
editorials.passage:
In July, a leading brand valuation consultancy had put Tata as India’s most valuable brand — for the 18th year in a row. It argued that the continued success of the Tata Group reflects the broader resilience of India’s branded economy. However, corporate shenanigans that followed weeks after the publication of the report did little to do justice to this storied brand, which evokes trust and respect for millions of Indians. Noel N. Tata, the chairman of Tata Trusts which owns 66% share of Tata Sons, the main holding company of the more than a century old Tata empire spanning across salt to semiconductors, was outmanoeuvred in a board meeting of Tata Sons that led to the selection of Natarajan Chandrasekaran as chairman of the holding company for a third five-year term. There are indications that a long-drawn court battle will ensue and the tangible impact of the feud will be decided in judicial tests.

Assuming fair play and that no actor beyond the Tata Group is playing behind the scene, the best or even the quickest of outcomes of the tussle between the shareholders — Tata Trusts — and the management — Tata Sons — may hurt the Tata brand. It did not become India’s most valuable brand on the basis of material metrics, such as revenue or market capitalisation. The value of the brand is derived from notions that the Tata Group is well governed, transparent, conducts business ethically and with a high level of intellectual integrity. This is the basis on which customers, suppliers, regulators, and employees affix the premium on the Group. This intangible premium remains equally relevant to the management as well as to regulatory bodies, governments, international investors, and the community at large. Unsurprisingly, more than a dozen foreign companies had partnered the Tatas in joint ventures after the economic liberalisation as they figured out that the Group was a cut above the rest when it came to governance, transparency, fairness, professionalism and long-term commitment. This is not to suggest that the Tata Group has been shorn of scars: the tiffs among Russi Mody, Darbari Seth and Ratan Tata in the 1990s and the public spat between Cyrus Mistry and Ratan Tata in 2016 are cases in point. Whether the current unfolding saga will prove to be just another unsavoury chapter in the Tata Group’s long history of corporate battles remains to be seen.

editorials.title: Icy warning: Editorial on the Himalayan fragility and India’s looming water crisis
editorials.passage:
The glacial lake outburst flood in Nepal last month that killed around 1,410 people and caused widespread destruction was a warning written in stone and sludge. The devastation, however, is only part of a larger crisis. A recent report titled A resilient Himalaya: protecting a region at risk and securing future prosperity , compiled by the global consultancy firm, Systemiq, in partnership with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development and G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, has drawn attention to the accelerating loss of ice in the Himalayas. It has alerted that Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago. The Himalayas could reach “peak water” — the point after which river flows begin to decline — by the middle of the century. By 2100, the Hindu Kush Himalayas could lose up to 80% of their present glacier volume.

For India, the portentous challenges will be environmental and economic. Diminishing water security would have severe consequences. The Himalayas feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems that, in turn, support agriculture, industry and livelihoods downstream. Worryingly, the Centre had informed Parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as “very high risk” following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The economic implications of such a finding are grim. The latest report estimates that Rs 64.8 lakh crore, or 21.5% of India’s GDP, is dependent on the Himalayas. Even though this does not mean that an Armageddon in the Himalayas would wipe out over 20% of India’s GDP, the economy’s dependence on this mountain range makes it vulnerable to disruptions. Farmers need steady water for cultivation. Cities need reliable supplies for households and industry. Hydropower projects require functioning river systems. A disruption to any of these can lead to a hydra-headed crisis. The collective response — all nation-states affected by the crisis — should transcend disaster relief. Glacial lakes require continuous monitoring. Yet, only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are currently being monitored. Construction in fragile mountain zones must face stricter scrutiny. Furthermore, black carbon, the report also highlighted, is driving the glacial melt. Reducing emissions from diesel engines, coal-burning industries, biomass cooking and open burning should form the pillars of India’s climate strategy.

editorials.title: Permanence of life insurance
editorials.passage:
A fixed deposit matures in five years; an equity share can be sold tomorrow. A whole life policy taken out by a father naming his newborn son may not discharge its obligation for 70 years. An immediate annuity bought at 30 pays as long as the annuitant lives — beyond a 100, if he lives that long. These are not rare cases. They are the product. And they change what regulation must do.

Most people assume insurance regulation exists to protect policyholders from bad companies — fraud, mismanagement, insolvency. That is incomplete. It exists to protect the contract from the mortality of companies. Companies fail, merge, restructure and exit markets. The contract can do none of these things; it must survive whatever happens to the institution that wrote it. That is the organising principle behind every provision governing mergers, amalgamations, portfolio transfers, run-offs and winding-up in life insurance law, in India and abroad.

The Insurance Act, 1938 addresses this in a cluster of provisions often cited but rarely explained. Under Section 35, no life insurance business may be transferred or amalgamated with that of another insurer except under a scheme approved by IRDAI. Section 36 goes further: before approving one, IRDAI must send notice to every life policyholder concerned and hear any who applies to be heard. The policyholder is not a passive party to a corporate transaction but a stakeholder whose voice must be heard. Section 37A empowers IRDAI to prepare a scheme of amalgamation itself, without waiting for the companies to propose one, if it is satisfied that the public interest, policyholders’ interests, or an insurer’s sound management requires it; the insurer taking over must consent in writing. This is an active intervention power, not a passive supervisory one.

Whatever such a scheme does to the company, Section 37A(4A) fixes what it cannot do to the policyholder: he is to have the same interest in, and rights against, the insurer that emerges as he had in the one he started with. Shareholders whose rights come out lower are compensated. Policyholders are not, because theirs do not change.

Run-off is the quietest version of the same duty. An insurer closed to new business must go on servicing the policies it has already written, for as long as they last, with no fresh premium arriving to make it convenient.

Beneath all this is a structural requirement: the life fund. Under Section 10, a life insurer must keep a separate life insurance fund, which stands as the security of the life policyholders, and cannot be applied for any other purpose. Section 56 carries that logic into failure. In a winding-up or an insolvency, the life assets and liabilities must be valued separately from everything else, and those assets cannot be applied to any other liability except to the extent they exceed the life liabilities. Other creditors reach them only after the policyholders have been answered.

IRDAI’s July 30, 2026, amendment to its registration and amalgamation regulations goes further still: where a non-insurance holding company is amalgamated into an insurer, solvency ratio after the amalgamation must stay above the 150 per cent control level.

This is not an India-specific narrative. In the UK, a transfer of insurance business under Part VII of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 needs the sanction of the High Court, in place of each policyholder’s consent. An Independent Expert, approved by the regulator, reports on its effect on policyholders, who are notified and may be heard. The court’s concern is not corporate convenience but whether any class of policyholder would be worse off.

In the US, state guaranty associations catch the policies of a member life insurer that fails: the surviving insurers are assessed to fund covered claims. The cover is not unlimited and limits vary by state, but the obligation does not vanish with the company.

India has lived this at its most dramatic scale. The nationalising ordinance of January 19, 1956, brought in 245 entities — Indian insurers, non-Indian insurers and provident societies. They were not shut down and replaced. Their life business, with its policies and liabilities, vested in the Life Insurance Corporation when it was formed on September 1 that year. Policyholders who had bought contracts from companies whose names they knew woke up as LIC policyholders. They may not have noticed. That was precisely the point.

HDFC Life describes its October 14, 2022, merger with Exide Life as the first M&A transaction in the sector. It came in two stages: the acquisition completed on January 1, 2022, then the amalgamation, sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai and approved by IRDAI. By the company’s account the whole transaction, from the September 2021 announcement, took under 14 months. The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, in force since February 5, 2026, extends the discipline into new territory, bringing mergers between insurers and non-insurance companies expressly within IRDAI’s prior approval. It also raises the FDI limit to 100 per cent, increasing ownership complexity and making the architecture that protects the contract within it more critical, not less.

The clearest proof either of us has seen came from one author’s service in Kenya, where he processed a claim on a whole-life policy issued by the Nairobi branch of the Oriental Government Security Life Assurance Company in the late 1930s. From the records available to us, the policy ran through India’s Independence in 1947 and Kenya’s in 1963 without interruption. When LIC was formed in 1956, Oriental’s obligations passed to its East Africa Division. In 1978, when Kenya required foreign insurers to incorporate locally, the Indian insurers there merged into Kenindia Assurance Company Ltd, born in Nairobi that December, and the portfolio passed to it. The claim was settled at Kenindia in 2013 — some 75 years after the policy was written, across the independence of two nations, one nationalisation, a change of sovereign law and three institutional transfers.

Not one of those discontinuities reduced the obligation. The contract simply continued, as contracts must be in systems built to keep them. That is what this architecture exists for: not the protection of companies, but the protection of promises.

Kumar is former Managing Director, and Sudhakar is former Executive Director, LIC. Views expressed are personal. Except where drawn from the authors’ own service records, all data are from publicly available sources

editorials.title: Food business must look beyond economic gain
editorials.passage:
A food business cannot just be a business; it has to be more. A few months ago, I said this to my neighbour in a casual conversation over tea. We rarely ask a food business what kind of world it is helping create; we ask whether it is profitable, scalable and competitive. Perhaps that is precisely where our thinking about food needs to change. I remember he sat back in his chair and began to smile, as if he had never heard something like that before.

His reaction stayed with me because it revealed how easily we have separated food from everything that gives it meaning. By definition, a business is a commercial activity: buying and selling goods and services for economic gain. Food, too, is a source of significant economic activity. But unlike most commodities, food enters our bodies, shapes our health, sustains livelihoods and connects us to the natural world. Its consequences extend far beyond the balance sheet.

The worldwide food economy is worth $10 trillion and is growing at 6 per cent annually. Globally, nearly 1.23 billion people work in food, across agriculture, fish and forest production, processing, packaging, transportation, stores and restaurants.

But food is much more. It is a fundamental source of life; it has an interdependent relationship with biodiversity and is integral to innumerable cultures. At every step of the value chain, when food is grown, processed, distributed, consumed and even disposed of, it impacts public health, environmental health, livelihoods and cultural heritage.

Having access to healthy food for children is not simply business; it is crucial to how they will live the rest of their lives. Looking after soil, animals, birds and pollinators is not simply business; it keeps biodiversity alive and maintains nature’s fine balance. Paying fair prices to growers and producers is not just business; it is the right thing to do. Sharing festival foods with the community is an act of love; it surely is not business.

Food is one of the richest human experiences and our constant connection to the rest of the planet. Why, then, has the food industry become comfortable with treating food merely as a product for economic gain? What would happen if food businesses began measuring their success by the health of the ecosystems, people and communities that sustain them?

Recent inspections by Food and Drug Administrations across India have attracted public attention, with spoiled or expired food seized from reputed eateries and establishments found non-compliant in food safety, hygiene and waste management. These are table stakes, the absolute bare minimum for any establishment working with food. Yet compliance, by definition, is the floor. It cannot be the ceiling of our ambition for food.

The real opportunity for any food business is to improve health, strengthen livelihoods, protect biodiversity and celebrate cultures. The question is no longer simply whether a food business is doing harm. It is whether it can actively create good.

For India, this is particularly consequential. We are one of the world’s largest food producers, home to extraordinary agricultural and culinary diversity, while also confronting malnutrition, lifestyle diseases, food waste, water stress and rapidly changing consumption patterns. Our food businesses sit at the centre of many of these contradictions and have an opportunity to become part of their solution.

FAO’s Strategic Framework 2022-31 characterises a resilient and sustainable food system through four pillars: better production, better nutrition, better environment and better life. Around the world, institutions and food businesses are beginning to redefine what responsible food systems can look like. The World Association of Chefs Societies’ ‘Feed the Planet’ initiative promotes sustainable food practices, while the Relais & Châteaux group has made commitments around sustainable farming, biodiversity and protecting local culinary heritage.

The lesson is not that every food business needs to replicate these commitments. It is that ambition can be deliberately designed into the business model rather than added later as a sustainability initiative.

So, what does this philosophy look like when translated into everyday business decisions?

Companies can begin by examining five dimensions: sourcing strength, including transparent supply chains and fair prices for producers; product integrity, including nutritional quality, seasonality and ingredients; operational impact, including water, energy, transportation, packaging and waste; people practices, including pay, training and inclusion; and customer experience, including transparency and responsiveness.

The purpose is not to create another sustainability scorecard. It is to help businesses see the connections between decisions often treated as separate.

Some changes can be simple: better food-waste management, shorter supply chains for local ingredients, greater transparency with consumers and sustainability training for teams. Bigger shifts in how products and services are designed can follow over time. Building and running a sustainable food business cannot be an overnight shift. But it is the need of the hour, and it can be done with the right leadership mindset, tools, capabilities, passionate teams and discipline.

While businesses focus on optimisation, value extraction and efficiency, the future belongs to quality, value regeneration and inclusion so that consumers can truly say from their hearts, “ Annadata sukhi bhava ” — may the hand that feeds us be forever blessed.

The writer is Co-Founder, Foodwize

editorials.title: What should India’s long term energy priorities be?
editorials.passage:
India’s economic growth is vitally linked to using more energy. Higher output in industry, transport, agriculture, and even the production of services needs more energy. Further, economic growth increases people’s demand for energy to power their appliances. Thus, there’s a need to boost India’s total energy supply every year, and this increasing supply must be affordable and resilient.

Further, India is committed to fighting climate change by reducing its greenhouse gas emissions, which, in turn, means reducing the use of fossil fuels. And that’s another powerful reason to reduce the economy’s dependence on imported oil and natural gas.

These structural features of the energy sector define India’s long-run energy priorities.

First, India has become extremely dependent on LPG cooking, and must now quickly shift to other fossil fuels. This will reduce reliance on a problematic fuel. First, LPG is largely imported, causing a stress on the country’s foreign exchange. Second, LPG is subsidised for lower-income households, creating a substantial burden on government finances. And third, LPG use adds to greenhouse gas emissions.

Making households shift from LPG cooking will not be easy as it is convenient and, unlike wood or coal, it does not produce smoke. And the many households now connected to LPG are unlikely to give it up unless better alternatives are made available. Hence, the government and research institutions should prioritise the development of alternatives.

The shift away from LPG is all the more important for establishments like dhabas and restaurant that prepare food on a large scale.

Currently, there aren’t many non-fossil-fuel alternatives to LPG. However, good progress has been made in the use of solar power for large-scale cooking.

For example, the Brahma Kumaris use solar energy to prepare thousands of meals every day at their Mount Abu facility.

It is likely that the shift away from LPG will be led by non-profit groups. So, it is important that experts help them to make the shift.

Energy storage should be another focus area. Without cheap, plentiful storage, full use of renewable energy cannot be made. This is because renewable energy is a flow and is available only intermittently, not 24x7.

At present, there are two major ways to store renewable energy: in batteries and as green hydrogen. Batteries will surely be needed for large scale renewable electricity generation; battery-based electric vehicles are already well-known. What is perhaps less known is that hydrogen-powered forklifts and long-distance buses are already in use in India.

To make significant progress in energy storage, strong financial support and promotion from the government will be required.

Third, India needs to promote energy efficiency in homes, offices, factories, shops, and transport. The Central and State governments already have various energy efficiency schemes. But these are not getting the kind of backing being given to solar power. This is the case even though it is well known that properly run energy-efficiency schemes are more cost effective than solar power.

Hence, the burden of promoting energy efficiency would largely fall on motivated non-profit groups.

The writer is an economist with extensive public policy experience

editorials.title: Below the Line
editorials.passage:
Spotted at GFF 2026 was Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, taking aim at India’s premier league of professional party-poopers or as she wryly called them, the “Naraaz Phupha ji s ” (the chronically offended wedding uncles) of economic commentary.

Addressing a room packed with high-octane innovators, the Minister noted that India’s youth boom isn’t a distant prophecy, it’s an active, high-definition reality. Yet, a certain vintage breed of commentators remains stubbornly committed to viewing a 21st-century digital surge through a 20th-century dial-up lens.

“To borrow the now so famous, in social media at least, expression which the honourable Prime Minister used, our Naraaz Phupha ji s are never short of reasons to doubt India’s momentum and capabilities of our youth. Spending their time debating in television studios, whether the demographic dividend has slipped away or turned into a burden. They rely on vibe casting, feel-casting rather than actual numbers,” she said. While these angry uncles are busy throwing tantrums, Gen Z is already writing tomorrow’s code, launching massive enterprises.

Aviation services are hitting a ‘new high’ every passing day under the watchful eyes of the Aviation Ministry. Recently, Akasa Air’s Goa-Mumbai flight was to land at T2 in Mumbai, then a message was sent it will land at T1.

A smart traveller told his driver to park between T1 and T2 and prayed that the aircraft lands safely. With the government deciding to shift the prevailing airport to a new Navi Mumbai location which is about 42 km from the old airport, only God can save the passengers.

A Chennai-based company recently hosted what its public relations billed to the media as a ‘roundtable’ on its products. Invitations were sent to multiple media outlets and a few reporters made their way to the event location. As they entered the conference hall, there was, in fact, a table, which was also round, but the faces around it seemed oddly unfamiliar. It was in fact organised for an internal customer meet and greet session, with the firm’s product heads holding discussions with its enterprise clients.

So, a few journalists sat quietly (outside the roundtable) in complete awkwardness.

A minister’s recent advice to officials to undertake ‘surprise’ visits to monitor a key scheme triggered more surprise than perhaps intended. Stakeholders wondered why an important ministry remains without a full-time dedicated minister, with insiders claiming the minister has rarely been a regular presence there over the past two years. With staff already stretched, one village-level stakeholder suggested the minister first tap his party network to identify alleged irregularities. An officer pointed out that surprise inspections are part of the guidelines.

The irony? Senior officials overseeing the scheme are reportedly reluctant to acknowledge deficiencies flagged by another ministry which is also handled by the same minister.
