Only the previous month, the National Green Tribunal dismissed challenges to the construction of a mega-infrastructure project on the island, asserting that no part of the project site is a CRZ-1A area – a category of coastal land that has maximum protection under law on account of its ecological importance.

Now, official records from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands Forest Department accessed via a Right to Information application have confirmed the Scroll report.

The March report, based on photographs accessed from Galathea Bay and from conversations with locals, had suggested about 1,000 turtle nests in the area over the November to March nesting period.

The data obtained via the RTI application puts the number of nests in Galathea Bay beach at 997, with 889 being of the leatherback turtle. The other 108 are of the Olive Ridley turtle.

These are numbers for the nests that have been re-located from the beach to the protected hatcheries that are managed by forest staff. The actual number of nests created on the beach is likely to be higher because not all nests are always located and moved.

This is the highest number of leatherback nests recorded in Galathea Bay since turtle monitoring began about four decades ago. The highest earlier was for the 2022 nesting season, which documented 649 nests of the leatherback and 31 of the Olive Ridley.

The leatherback is the largest and deepest diving of the seven species of marine turtles that inhabit the oceans of the planet. Leatherbacks are divided into seven sub-populations. The ones that nest in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands constitute the Northeast Indian Ocean population.

This sub-population, according to a recent paper in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science , is also one of least studied of the seven sub-populations of this species.

The lead author of the paper, Maslim As-singkily, a researcher in marine turtle ecology and population genetics, told Scroll that this latest data confirms Galathea as the beach with highest-recorded leatherback nests in the region for a single season.

“Galathea is an exceptionally productive reproductive habitat today,” said As-singkily, who is also a member of the International Union for Conservation of Nature Species Survival Commission’s Indonesia Species Specialist Group. “The 889 nests are particularly striking compared with the other leatherback nesting populations I have assessed across the Northeast Indian Ocean [Sumatra, Malaysia and Thailand].”

He said that the information puts Galathea Bay “in a comparable range to some of the other important leatherback nesting beaches in the Western Pacific, for example, Wermon Beach [Jeen Syuaib] in Papua, Indonesia”.

Wermon and Jamursba Medi in the same province in Indonesia have been recognised as major leatherback nesting beaches in the western Pacific but have experienced “substantial long-term declines”, As-singkily said.

Significantly, Galathea Bay is the site of the approximately Rs 50,000-crore transshipment port proposed as part of the mega infrastructure push by the Indian government.

The port is the centre-piece of the larger Rs 92,000-crore project that includes an airport, a power plant and a greenfield township and tourism facilities over 130 sq km of primarily pristine evergreen forests.

The port project entails constructing breakwaters that will reduce the opening of Galathea Bay by 90% – from 3,000 metres wide currently to a mere 300 meters. This is likely to have a very significant impact on this nesting site of global importance.

“Constructing a port directly within Galathea Bay will involve extensive dredging, construction of breakwaters, coastal reclamation, light pollution, and vessel traffic,” said another sea turtle biologist, requesting anonymity. “This will directly destroy or render inaccessible one of the region’s important leatherback nesting beaches.”

However, he noted that leatherbacks can shift nesting beaches within a geographic region and “that individuals displaced from Galathea, will likely attempt to nest on other adjacent beaches in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands or the western coast of Sumatra as was seen after the tsunami of 2004”.

But Hiltrud Cordes of the Turtle Foundation, which also works extensively in the region, is worried about this argument. “A sudden loss of a key nesting beach through a massive construction poses a big threat to a vulnerable nesting population,” she said. “Nesting beaches in Sumatra are themselves not a safe place for sea turtles. Even though all species of sea turtles are protected by law in Indonesia, there is a high level of poaching of eggs and turtles for their meat."

The nesting numbers in Galathea Bay underscore the legal violations that have been allowed in support of the project. Turtle nesting sites qualify for the highest levels of protection as a coastal regulation zone-1A site. Large development projects such as a port cannot even be considered here, a fact that the National Green Tribunal ignored completely when passing its final order in February dismissing all concerns on ecological and legal grounds related to the project.

The 2026 nesting records of the Leatherback “make it imperative that the Galathea nesting ground is safeguarded under any circumstances” said BC Choudhury, a former head of Endangered Species Management Department of Wildlife Institute of India and an IUCN SSC Marine Turtle Specialist Group Member. “It shows why the development sector should not go blind to the truth.”

Choudhury added, “There is always the possibility of compromise and alternatives that permits both development and conservation to go hand in hand but only if the development proponents respect the historical and current scientific opinions just a little bit more.”

Scroll emailed Dinesh Kannan, principal conservator of forests, wildlife, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, requesting a response to this information.

A similar query was sent to Deepak Apte, former Director Bombay Natural History Society and chair of the environment ministry’s environment appraisal committee that oversaw the environment clearance to the project in November 2022. Apte currently serves as the biodiversity expert on the monitoring committee formed to oversee biodiversity related matters as per the environment clearance granted to the project. This article will be updated if they respond.

Pankaj Sekhsaria is the recipient of the Prem Bhatia Environment Journalism Award 2026 for his research and writing on the Great Nicobar mega infrastructure project. He is the author/editor of seven books on the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, the latest being The Great Nicobar Betrayal (Frontline, 2024) and Island on Edge - The Great Nicobar Crisis (Westland, 2025).

editorials.title: Indian writer Ruthvika Rao wins £10,000 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize for ‘The Fertile Earth’
editorials.passage:
The winner of the 2026 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize is The Fertile Earth by Ruthvika Rao. She will receive a cash prize of £10,000.

The Prize celebrates the outstanding adventure fiction written in English by authors of any nationality and published in paperback in the UK. The winner was chosen by librarians and library staff, and by professionals whose work is between adventure and storytelling.

In The Fertile Earth, Vijaya and Sree are the daughters of the Deshmukhs of Irumi. Hailing from a lineage of ancestral aristocrats, their family’s social status and power over villagers on their land are absolute. Krishna and Ranga, brothers, are the sons of a widowed servant in the Deshmukh household. When Vijaya and Krishna meet, they forge an intense bond that is beautiful and dangerous. But after an innocent attempt to hunt down a man-eating tiger in the jungle goes wrong, what happens between the two of them is disastrous, with the consequences reverberating through their lives into young adulthood.

A review on Scroll said, “Rao’s prose brings alive the social hierarchies in the village of Irumi situated in the Eastern Ghats… The Fertile Earth captures a country in the throes of an explosive rise of violent Naxalite movements seeking to restore justice to a post-independent India plagued with cruelty and feudalism.”

editorials.title: Russian polls over, Ukraine war enters a dangerous new phase
editorials.passage:
Ukraine reportedly launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia on Sunday, including hundreds directed towards Moscow. The attacks were timed to coincide with the third and final day of parliamentary elections in the country. If reports are to be believed, it was the largest drone assault ever recorded against the Russian capital.
This may be the most dangerous escalation in the Ukraine war and may mark a watershed moment in the intensity and scale of the conflict.

Wars are notoriously difficult to predict, more so when someone like Vladimir Putin is involved. Despite being at the centre of Russian and global affairs for more than 25 years, Putin remains one of the world’s most scrutinised yet frequently misunderstood leaders. But given the trajectory of this war, and the manner in which Europe is preparing for a prolonged confrontation with Moscow, the prospect of a wider conflict can no longer be dismissed.

Maybe this is part of the calculation in Kiev and some Western European capitals. Escalation could force Washington to abandon the Trump administration’s ambivalence and commit more decisively to Ukraine. Those who believe Putin’s position is weakening may see sustained pressure on Russia as the route to a Ukrainian victory and, ultimately, to uprooting Putin’s rule.

That could prove a grave miscalculation. Ukraine has already been devastated by more than four years of war. For President Volodymyr Zelenskyy personally, the political stakes are enormous. He knows well that Russia won’t settle for anything short of total victory and the permanent enfeeblement of Kiev so that it can never be used by the West to mount future offensives against Moscow. This would be political suicide for him. Continued war, therefore, carries a different political calculus for Zelenskyy than it does for Europe.

Europe has much more to lose from an uncontrolled escalation. And that is where misreading Russia — and Putin — could prove disastrous.

Russia undoubtedly faces severe pressures. Its economy is strained, and the human cost of the war has been immense. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimates that the Russian military suffered about 1.4 million battlefield casualties, including as many as 450,000 deaths, between February 2022 and June 2026.
During World War II, the erstwhile Soviet Union lost between 8 lakh and 10 lakh soldiers, and 24 million civilians. Germany came second on the list, with the loss of 5,533,000 soldiers and 66-88 lakh civilians. In sharp contrast, the US lost 416,800 soldiers and 418,500 civilians, the UK suffered 383,600 military losses and 450,700 civilian deaths, and France suffered 217,600 military casualties and 567,600 civilian deaths. It won’t be far-fetched to say that the Allied forces won the war against the German alliance largely by relying on Russian sacrifices.

For a country that valorises sacrifice and sees Ukraine as its lifeline, losing 450,000 soldiers is huge, but still seen as an unavoidable casualty. Western experts and commentators analysing the Ukraine war merely through battlefield losses may not be reading the Russian situation correctly.

Another problem with Western media and academia is that they largely live and work in echo chambers, far removed from Russian realities. Reports of economic stress, fuel shortages and public dissatisfaction are plentiful and, arguably, vastly exaggerated. Political scientist John Mearsheimer, after a recent visit to Russia, offered a strikingly different assessment in a podcast. “The Russian economy is in quite good shape,” he said. The only real impact he saw of the sanctions “in terms of having a negative effect on Russia were the lines at a number of petrol stations or what we here in the United States call gas stations. I saw a number of lines of cars at different gas stations”.

More significantly, Mearsheimer said he saw no evidence of an impending uprising against Putin. If anything, he saw “lots of people in the national security elite inside of Russia who felt that Putin was not waging the war vigorously enough” and that “the Russians are determined to continue escalating until they bring Ukraine to its knees”.

The assumption that Putin’s departure would automatically produce a more accommodating Russia, Mearsheimer argued, amounts to “living in a dream world”. He added: “If Putin were to be removed from office or if Putin were to have a massive heart attack tomorrow and pass away, the person who would replace him in all likelihood would be a real hardliner — someone who is inclined to be even tougher in terms of waging the Ukraine war than Putin has been and even is now.”
This brings us to the second part of the problem: that the West may be misreading Putin himself.

In his book We Need to Talk About Putin, author Mark Galeotti writes: “There’s snow, there are bears, there’s vodka — and then there’s chess, one of the irritatingly durable clichés for Russia and Russians. Consider the classic Russian film villains: there’s the brutish thug, of course, but there’s also the unemotional chess player, ten moves ahead of his rival.”

Putin, too, is projected either as a “crazy S.O.B.”, as Joe Biden saw him, or “a thug, a murderer and a killer”, as Senator John McCain called him, or a “three-dimensional chess” player, as Hillary Clinton thought.

Galeotti offers a different metaphor. He says that Putin is far less a “chess player” and more of “a judoka”. He writes: “Chess is a contest of inflexible rules, transparency and an intellectual competition where the options are strictly constrained… Putin doesn’t want to limit his options like that. He does know judo, however… A judoka may well have prepared for a rival’s usual moves and worked out countermoves in advance, but much of the art is in using the opponent’s strength against him to seize the moment when it appears. In this respect, in geopolitics, as in judo, Putin is an opportunist... He relies on quickly seizing any disadvantage he sees, rather than on a careful strategy.”

Putin also has to be seen in the Russian context. As his biographer Philip Short writes in Putin: His Life and Times, Putin “is no more an aberration in Russia than Donald Trump in America, Boris Johnson (who was British prime minister at the time of the book’s publication), or Emmanuel Macron in France. He represents the hopes and fears, the aspirations and anguish, the conceits and resentments of a substantial part of the Russian population, who regularly support him”.

This is precisely why assumptions about a post-Putin Russia can be dangerous. Removing the man would not necessarily remove the forces that produced him.
Post-results, Putin may be forced to go the hard way. Zelenskyy may have his reasons to escalate the war, but can the same be said about European leaders, who are busy fuelling the war machine in Ukraine? What they forget is that Putin’s political instincts were shaped by the street culture of post-war Leningrad. As author Richard Lourie writes in Putin: His Downfall and Russia’s Coming Crash: “The lesson that the streets of Leningrad taught was simple, and it stayed with Putin his whole life: The weak get beaten. Weakness is both disgrace and danger.”

That street code shaped Putin’s worldview and his political tactics. “The streets of Leningrad taught me one thing: if a fight is unavoidable, throw the first punch,” the Russian president would concede much later in an interview. Today, as the Ukraine war intensifies and the West gears up for war, Putin seems to be veering towards the idea that a fight with the West is inevitable, and he might be tempted to throw the first punch.

The West also needs to realise that if Putin’s street-fight tactics make him a dangerous adversary, equally decisive is the unique place Ukraine occupies in the Russian historical imagination. “All Russian history flowed from Kiev. Every schoolchild learned: Kiev is the mother of Russian cities, Ukraine is Russia’s breadbasket,” Lourie writes.

None of this justifies Russia’s invasion. But it helps explain why Moscow attaches vastly greater historical, strategic and emotional significance to Ukraine than many Western capitals traditionally do. For Putin — and Russia — Ukraine is not merely another piece on the geopolitical chessboard; it is intertwined with his idea of Russia. This makes compromise harder.

There was a period when Putin sought accommodation with the West. During his early years in power, he repeatedly described Russia as part of European civilisation, pursued closer cooperation with Washington after 9/11, and publicly entertained much closer relationships with Nato and the European Union. But the EU and America refused to take Russia in. The eastward expansion of Nato created a further divide. In the process, the US-led West not only lost a potential ally in Putin, especially against a rising China, but also created a formidable adversary in Russia.
Today, as Putin wins yet another election, the Ukraine war enters a far more dangerous phase. What’s even more worrying is that this time the West, and not just Ukraine, should brace for Putin’s ‘punch’.

(Utpal Kumar is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The Mecca pact: India must build alternative security architectures
editorials.passage:
The Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and subsequent claims that even the holy city of Mecca was targeted have raised fresh questions about the efficacy and operationalisation of the Mecca pact. The fact that the attack on Saudi Arabia did not elicit any response from Pakistan or Turkey — apart from mere statements — shows that the accord signed in Mecca on August 7 is still awaiting operationalisation.

The pact that ostensibly treats “attack on one as an attack on all three” and was projected as “Islamic Nato” has proved to be a hollow alignment, with lots of hype and little substance. However, both Pakistan and Turkey have reiterated that the pact would be operationalised. It may be a mere bluster, but from an Indian perspective, needs to be taken seriously. While one must not get traumatised by it, trivialising it would a grave blunder.
What the Mecca pact is — and why it matters
The Mecca pact builds on a 2025 Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and extends that to Turkey. A joint statement issued after the summit highlighted that an armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all. Its text emphasises collective deterrence against aggression and provides for enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation. It was deliberately signed in Mecca to invoke a potent religious symbol, with an aim of drawing other Islamic countries into the pact. Pakistan already has a defence pact with Somalia and there are reports of other countries considering this security arrangement.

The strategic logic is one of complementarities: Saudi Arabia brings financial heft and energy wealth; Turkey brings a robust defence-industrial base and a thriving drone industry; Pakistan brings a large armed force backed by a burgeoning population. In addition, the symbolism of Saudi Arabia as the custodian of two holy mosques, Turkey as the successor of last caliphate, and Pakistan as the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority nation coming together could create a natural attraction for it in the larger Islamic world, which has for long lamented the loss of their medieval glory. The trio are now institutionalising the arrangement, with a secretariat in Riyadh and a committee mechanism that met recently in Istanbul.
Expansion scenarios and the Bangladesh question
The pact’s architects have left room for expansion, and names such as Egypt and some Gulf states have been floated in public discussion. Bangladesh has signalled interest and says it sees “no risk” in joining, arguing participation would not preclude other partnerships. Dhaka notes that it has yet to receive a formal invitation, but the possibility remains a live topic as the alliance’s first committee meetings define its scope.

From India’s standpoint, Bangladesh’s accession would be the most consequential near-term variable. Geographically encircled by India and heavily dependent on Indian transit and trade, Bangladesh joining a collective-defence bloc that includes Pakistan alters the strategic calculus on India’s eastern flank. It need not be framed as an immediate military threat, but it is a security issue that warrants clear signalling: India should convey its displeasure at any move that could, over time, assume an anti-India posture.
Why the US and China welcome it — for different reasons
Washington’s public welcome reflects purely a materialistic desire of the Trump Administration to get rid of the regional security burdens. Beijing’s welcome is rooted in a different calculation: the pact draws Turkey—a Nato member—and two key U.S. partners closer together in a framework that reduces their dependence on the U.S, while reducing the latter’s presence in West Asia.
The UAE factor and India’s opportunity
One major Gulf power has so far shown little inclination to join: the UAE. Abu Dhabi appears to prefer banking on India for its security umbrella rather than subsuming itself in a Saudi-led compact. That creates an opening for India, which has the wherewithal to provide credible security and has historical linkages across the Gulf; many of these emirates were administered from British India, and India has long looked after their security interests.

If India actively engages the UAE’s security expectations, other Gulf states may become more comfortable joining an India-led defence compact than one with Pakistan. This need not be a formal alliance that compromises India’s strategic autonomy; it can be a network of bilateral security umbrellas for smaller Indian Ocean and Gulf states that house large Indian diasporas and seek protection without ideological alignment.
Iran, Israel and the limits of a ‘hexagon’
The Mecca signatories have stressed that the pact is defensive and not directed at any specific country, and even Iran has not criticised it openly. Some in Pakistan have speculated about eventually bringing Iran into the framework, though conflicting interests make that uncertain. Iran requires a different approach. Tehran should be reassured that India's emerging security partnerships in the Gulf are not directed against it, while high-level engagement with Iran continues. India's existing defence relationships with Israel, and its growing partnerships with Greece and Cyprus, can likewise be strengthened without attempting to construct a single grand security architecture encompassing all of them. A web of practical bilateral relationships may be more effective than an ambitious multilateral label that carries political costs for potential Gulf partners.
What India should do now
India should apply the same flexibility elsewhere. If Pakistan's defence partnership with Somalia continues to deepen, New Delhi should examine more closely its options in the Horn of Africa, including the possibility of recognising Somaliland and developing a defence partnership with it. The objective should be to preserve India's strategic position and maritime interests rather than to enter an open-ended contest of blocs.

At the same time, India should prepare for harder contingencies. If the logic of the Mecca pact eventually acquires a stronger operational dimension, Saudi Arabia and Turkey could acquire greater capacity to influence India's access to important Mediterranean and Red Sea corridors. India should therefore strengthen maritime contingency planning and ensure that its trade and strategic interests are not vulnerable to a changing regional security alignment.

The Mecca pact does not make Pakistan invulnerable, nor does a mutual-defence clause automatically translate into identical military commitments by all its members, as is clearly evident from the response to the recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. But its institutional momentum and potential for expansion create new strategic variables for India.

The answer is not to abandon strategic autonomy. It is to understand that autonomy is sustained by having options. India has been cautious in the Gulf, the Horn of Africa and its wider maritime neighbourhood for understandable reasons. The emerging security landscape requires a more active form of statecraft: deeper partnerships, clearer signalling, stronger maritime preparedness and a willingness to shape the regional balance rather than simply respond to it.
 
(Capt. [Dr.] Alok Bansal is the Executive Vice President of India Foundation. Yashowardhan Tiwari is a Program Manager at the VC Office, Rishihood University. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the authors. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: China Compass | Beyond Brics bonhomie: China’s India strategy and the US factor
editorials.passage:
Now that we are at some distance from the pomp and ceremony of the 18th Brics Summit hosted by New Delhi, it is perhaps easier to reflect and realise that while multilateralism is not quite dead, Brics remains less than the sum of the bilateral relations between its members. The most consequential of these for India remains its relationship with China. And here, the contrast between the length of the Brics Declaration and the brevity of the respective Indian and Chinese statements on the sidelines meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping tells a story in itself.
Indian Dependence
By contrast, some Chinese analysts of bilateral ties with India have been quite elaborate in their assessment of the Summit and the Modi-Xi meeting. One of the most important analyses is an interview in a Chinese online outlet of Hu Shisheng, the top South Asia expert at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, a think-tank under the Ministry of State Security that oversees China’s external intelligence operations.

Hu pointed out that India-China relations were not being reset as much as finding a floor below which they would not fall. He declared clearly what Chinese official statements only hint at – that this was “tactical rapprochement, not a strategic reconciliation”. Even so, he was at pains to dismiss Indian stress on what was effectively a heavily militarised boundary and the possible risks this entailed, stating that the two countries had moved from “crisis management” to “border management”. The effort is clearly to convince the Indians that the relationship is back on track and that continuing suspicions of China are unwarranted.

The need is portrayed as India’s — that its industrial modernisation and the international competitiveness of “Make in India” are dependent on continuing links with China’s production and supply chains. For Hu, the reality is not so much of India “replacing” China as of China helping upgrade India’s manufacturing and moving to “jointly building competitive production capacity and entering international markets.” The record, however — China’s export and visa controls against India in the wake of Galwan and the US trade war and attempts to decouple from China — shows the opposite.

Hu’s positive-sum approach stands in sharp contrast with the zero-sum language of China’s own official statements and must, therefore, be understood as simply a propaganda effort to incentivise those in India worried about its weak economic fundamentals and the desultory progress of “Make in India” to choose the immediate benefits of cooperation with China over the short-term pain but long-term wisdom of preparing against over-dependence on China.

This is not to say that Hu is pulling his punches on the balance of power between India and China — if the economic dependency were not clear, he underlines the “asymmetry in comprehensive national strength” in China’s favour and simultaneously highlights India’s difficult international environment by noting disruptions in US-India relations. Implied here is that it was inevitable that India would make its peace with China as a result.
US Factor
Given that Xi Jinping is soon to visit the US, how the Chinese see the US factor in their ties with India is worth exploring in greater detail. Hu highlights an American official’s statement at the Raisina Dialogue in March 2026 that the US would not allow India to repeat a ‘China-style rise’, grant it the kind of “preferential treatment” in terms of comprehensive market access and technology transfer that it had once provided to China, nor “repeat the strategic mistakes made with China.” For Hu, then — and it must be assumed for the Chinese foreign and security policy leadership to whom he sends his reports — there is little in India’s current actions that would allow it to overcome these strictures and economic limitations.

For his part, Hu rubs it in by noting three ways in which the US has increased pressure on India and, thus, forced the latter to fix ties with China. One, the Trump administration’s tariff crackdown on India and pressure on Russia-India energy cooperation; two, the pressure on India’s energy situation due to the Trump-induced conflict in West Asia; and three, the establishment of a “constructive strategic stability relationship” between the US and China during Trump’s May visit to China. Hu’s attempt is to show that the India-US relationship can never be as important to Washington DC as the US-China relationship, but he ignores similar pressures on China because of the first two factors and Beijing’s own lack of certainty about any promises that Trump makes.

Indeed, Beijing is not taking things easy at all. After some years of having limited his international travel, Xi took the effort to travel in the space of a few weeks to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, to Egypt and to the Brics Summit in India before he makes it to the US in less than a week from now, suggesting concerns at the highest levels about stabilising China’s own external environment. In pushing for closer economic linkages with India and stability in US-China relations, Beijing is trying to ensure that the large Indian economy is not entirely lost to its manufacturers and that China’s own path is not blocked or slowed by frictions in either of these two relationships or an alignment between India and the US. The US might have walked back from its formulation of the Indo-Pacific, but the fact that India was able to ensure a joint Brics declaration and to prevent plans for overt de-dollarisation that would have been read more seriously in Washington as anti-US than, say, the statement on Cuba, means that India still possesses a degree of diplomatic capacity that the Chinese worry about.

For now, however, the smooth conclusion of the 18th Brics Summit works well for China — it gives Xi a card to play in Washington and, no matter the state of either US-China ties or Sino-Indian relations, sets the stage for China’s chairmanship of Brics in the coming year and renewed efforts for an anti-US agenda and to sideline India.
 
(Jabin T. Jacob is Professor, Department of International Relations and Governance Studies, and Director, Centre of Excellence for Himalayan Studies, Shiv Nadar University, Delhi NCR. editorials.title: Trump’s New Weapon Against Russian Oil Buyers Puts India on Notice
editorials.passage: In February, the US Supreme Court had taken Donald Trump's tariff weapon away, but the US Congress has now handed him a more dangerous one.The Russia-Iran sanctions act, sponsored by Senator Lindsey Graham and signed into law by Trump on Friday, 18 September, allows tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian oil or help Moscow evade sanctions. India and China are the obvious targets of the law that takes effect in 30 days, and countries then have 180 days to comply.The US President will decide who is to be hit, at what rate, and who is gets a waiver. The statute is a loaded gun, but the safety is in Trump's hands and the potential targets in his eyes. Given the Trump style what probably matters is not the text of the law but his mood, towards India, the world, or Prime Minister Narendra Modi on any given day. New Delhi should plan for the worst case, because it imports 88 percent of its oil and Russia has been providing a large proportion of it in the past several years.The official MEA response has been to say nothing with great firmness, except to remind the press that India is "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" through "diversified sourcing" and "evolving market dynamics."The press note adds that the implications for the bilateral relationship and for the international energy market have been "very clearly articulated" to US interlocutors. This is the language of a government that is still trying to figure out what to do.US Senate Passes Russia Sanctions Bill, 100% Sanctions Threat Looms On IndiaDiversification is a comforting word except that the reality has been lopsided. Over the past year Russia has supplied between 30-50 percent of India's crude needs. In July, India bought a record 110.4 lakh tonnes worth $7.3 billion; in August, 85 lakh tonnes worth $4.7 billion.A country that once depended on Iraq and Saudi Arabia has been leaning on one supplier in recent years. Before the Ukraine war, Russia was a marginal source. Then sanctions arrived, discounts followed, and Western capitals quietly encouraged Indian purchases to keep global prices down. Giving up Russian oil is bound to hit India hard.India needs to figure out just what the Americans want. Certainly they have made it clear that they want us to stop buying Russian oil. There is every indication that they also want India to become big buyers of American products, including energy. But, instead of allowing market forces to operate, they are into coercion, pure and simple.In August 2025, they imposed 25 percent Russia-related sanctions on India while sparing China, the much bigger buyer. The tariff was only withdrawn when the Supreme Court threw out the Trump tariffs in February this year.Under the interim India-US trade framework deal the White House in early February, India had committed itself to diversifying its energy procurement away from Russia and was willing to buy $500 billion worth of energy products and agricultural goods from the US.In April, American ambassador Sergio Gor noted that trade discussions since have included pushes for India to satisfy its energy needs from the US and its (new) partners in Venezuela and Guyana.As a result of the US war on Iran and the closure of Hormuz, the US has already become a major supplier of LPG and LNG to India. India imported 3.78 million tonnes of LPG from the US just in the March-August 2026 period. In June this year the US has emerged as India’s top LNG supplier with a 28 percent year on year surge to 2.66 million tonnes. India has now begun signing long term contracts with US companies like US Gulf Coast company.Note that importing energy from the US to India carries a massive freight premium due to geography and global shipping trends. A typical voyage from West Asia takes around 4-7 days, while that from Texas to India will take 40-45 days.Now the Trump administration has overcome the hurdle of the Supreme Court and got an even stouter weapon to coerce India. Despite brave talk, New Delhi’s recent record in dealing with American pressure is not encouraging. Venezuela supplied 6.7 percent of India's oil in 2016-17. Trump sanctioned Caracas in 2019, India cut its imports within a year, and by 2021-22 they were zero. Now, with American encouragement, India is being encouraged to buy Venezuelan oil again.Iran supplied 10 percent of India's requirements before sanctions were reimposed in November 2018. Given its geographic proximity, its crude reaches Indian ports faster and cheaper than almost anyone's. Imports were zero by 2020-21. In the brief window Washington allowed between March and June 2026, Iran's share climbed back to 1.1 per cent. And now it is again zero.But the record is not always dismal. When Trump raised tariffs on India from 25 to 50 percent in August 2025, New Delhi did not capitulate. It cut Russian purchases slowly, enough to assuage Washington. And after US tariff authority was thrown out by the Supreme Court in February and the Strait of Hormuz closed, cutting off the route for 40 to 50 percent of India's oil, Russian imports climbed again. Nobody in Washington could make India stop, and nobody there had the will to try.On the Mat: India’s Self-Inflicted Trade Deal With Trump Will Haunt it for YearsNew Delhi's hand is markedly weaker than Beijing's. China holds rare earths and magnets that the American EV, robotics and defence industries cannot do without. It supplies over 70 per cent of America's active pharmaceutical ingredients and nearly 50 percent of its electronics and advanced hardware. It can retaliate in ways that hurt.All India offers Washington is a promise. The US sees India as an alternative to China in civilian manufacturing and technology supply chains, but this remains a work in progress. The Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET), which became TRUST in 2025 has joint projects in space and green energy which are yet to take off. India, meanwhile, still needs America as a key export market and a source of technology and finance.America's dependencies on India are geopolitical, and the Trump administration is discounting them. It is courting Beijing and ignoring the Quad. Its immigration crackdown erodes the value of the Indian talent pool that once made Indian students and migrants indispensable.Washington's indulgence has also been selective. Washington chose not to apply CAATSA sanctions over India's purchase of Russian military equipment. The waiver to Indian companies to operate Chahbahar port in Iran ran out in April.What should Delhi do in the 180 days? It should use them as a negotiating period, not a compliance deadline. It can stagger purchases so that the fall in Russian volumes is visible but gradual. Diplomatically it could make the case that Indian purchases of Russian oil at a discount have kept global prices lower than they would otherwise be.But if the US adopts a punitive approach in imposing tariffs, it could take a series of toucher measures. This could include counter-tariffs on high-value US goods and choke of its import of US agricultural goods like almonds apples and pulses. Tariffs could also be put on US machinery chemicals and medical devices all of which can be obtained from alternative European or Asian suppliers. It could expand rupee settlement and other arrangements that reduce exposure to dollar-based enforcement.US-India defence ties have been the key achievements on the entente between the two countries in the past quarter century. If the US severely penalises the Indian economy, India should cut back in its defence engagement with the US, restrict US defence purchases and downgrade its engagement with the Quad.India may have been firm about energy security in a press note. But as the clock has started ticking for the implementation of the Graham Act that can gut the Indian economy, it needs to show it has some steel as well.(The writer is a Distinguished Fellow, Observer Research Foundation, New Delhi.
